paras: The threatened lynching of Ben Boney and Willie Kirksey took place at Meridian, Mississippi, in August 1915, after the two Black men were arrested on the accusation of stopping a woman's buggy on the Causeyville road. With a crowd gathered and a lynching feared, the sheriff sent them out of the county under guard. Mississippi papers later reported that the two had been indicted and then found innocent, and carried the story as "Nearly Lynched Wrong Men."

On Sunday afternoon, August 15, Mrs. Curtis Robertson was returning to Meridian in a buggy with her baby from a visit to Causeyville. According to a Meridian dispatch in the Hattiesburg News, two armed men stepped into the road and ordered her to stop, and she drew a revolver from under the buggy cushion and fired four shots, hitting no one, before they fled. The Montgomery Advertiser's Meridian correspondent, who spelled her name "Robinson," wrote that Boney "made insulting remarks" and caught hold of her horse's bridle.

A posse caught Boney, 23, and Kirksey, 16, early Monday morning at the home of Sol Kirksey and placed them in the county jail. The Advertiser reported that Mrs. Robinson at first would not identify them, "fearing mob violence," because "quite a crowd had collected at the Kirksey home, breathing vengeance"; later on August 16 she positively identified them. Officers, as relayed by the Hattiesburg dispatch, would not say whether she had identified the men.

After dark the sheriff put the two prisoners in an automobile under heavy guard and sent them to another county, which the later state-news item named as Jackson. Officers let it be known that a lynching had been feared, but no demonstration was reported.

On August 20 a grand jury indicted Kirksey and Boney, and the same day James Whitehead and Norman Elliott, also Black, were arrested and jailed on the charge of attempting to assault Mrs. Robertson. According to the state-news item, it was soon found that Kirksey and Boney were innocent, and Whitehead and Elliott confessed while saying they had only asked her to let them ride and meant no harm. No report of the release of Kirksey and Boney or of a trial of Whitehead and Elliott was found.

Only white papers carried the case, and no Black-press coverage of it was found. The first reports took the accusation as settled: the Montgomery Advertiser headed its special "Mrs. Robinson Identifes Negroes Who Stopped Her" and called the incident an "attempted assault," while the Hattiesburg News ran "Negroes Spirited Away" under its "Mississippi News" heading. Neither paper commented on the crowd beyond reporting it.

A week later a syndicated state-news item, headed "Nearly Lynched Wrong Men" in the Port Gibson Reveille, the Oxford Eagle and the Greene County Herald, described "a case of mistaken identity that threatened a lynching." The Brandon News and the Brookhaven Semi-Weekly Leader ran the same text without that headline among state briefs, the Leader's copy breaking off before the grand jury. The item's headline raised the charge to "attempted criminal assault" and called Whitehead and Elliott "the guilty negroes," even as its text gave their account that they had only asked for a ride.

Accounts of the roadside encounter differ: a hold-up by two armed men in the Hattiesburg dispatch, insults and a seized bridle in the Montgomery special, and a request for a ride in the confessions reported later. The reports also differ on when the prisoners were moved, the state-news item giving the night of August 16 and the Hattiesburg dispatch, dated August 18, saying "last night."

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Boney and Willie Kirksey
bases: Two Black men accused of accosting a woman were held while a crowd gathered 'breathing vengeance' and the sheriff moved them out of the county because a lynching was feared; no one was killed, so it is a threatened lynching (A2, A3, A5).

A crowd gathered at the place of arrest and a mob was feared, but the sheriff moved the prisoners away and no one was killed or attacked (A2, A3, A5); this was a threatened lynching, not a lynching under the standard definition.

The Montgomery Advertiser special (A1, A2), the Hattiesburg News dispatch (A3) and the state-news item (A5) agree that Boney and Kirksey were arrested and that mob violence was feared; only the state-news item and its reprints report the indictment, the second arrests and the 'wrong men' finding.
